column1: # clues.tsv for rush — pedagogic hints only. NEVER state the expected value or the fix.
# Format: <hint><TAB><member CASE label><TAB>...   (fires if ANY member case fails)
# Lines are shown most-fundamental first; the first line doubles as the "foothold".
# Member labels are the CASE column of the tables: they come from cases.tsv and
# edge_cases.tsv, which are generated — rename a case there and rename it here.

Every character you print sits at some (row, column). Before writing a single loop, work out on paper, for one small rectangle, which positions get a corner, which get a wall, and which get a space. Every failure below is a disagreement between that table and your loops.

Count what you actually emitted: exactly y lines, each exactly x characters wide. If a whole family of sizes is off by one character or one line, suspect a loop bound rather than the characters -- and check that x and y are not doing each other's job.

When y is 1 the only row is both the first row and the last row; when x is 1 the only column is both the first column and the last one. Two rules claim the same cell, and only one may speak: the subject's own rush(1,1), rush(5,1) and rush(1,5) transcripts tell you which.

A rectangle 2 wide has no room for anything between its two corners, and one 2 tall has no room between its two corner rows -- a 2x2 is all corners. Can the loop that fills the space between corners legitimately run zero times?

Four corners can be four DIFFERENT characters -- compare the rush02, rush03 and rush04 chapters. Does the character you print at a corner depend on both which row and which column you are on, or only on one of them?

Everything strictly inside the border is a space, and the row still has to finish with its right-hand wall. The table escapes your output, so '\n' marks exactly where each line ended: a space sitting just before one means you printed a character too many.

Because the output is escaped, every newline you printed is visible in the table -- count them, and look at what comes after the very last one. A missing or an extra final newline is a KO on the Moulinette even when the picture looks right.

A zero or negative size is not an error you must report, but your loops still have to notice it. Does your row loop test its condition before the first row or only after it? And if you compute how many characters go between the corners, what is that value when x is 0 or 1 -- and in what type is it evaluated?

RUNAWAY OUTPUT means one call printed more than a megabyte. For a size like 0 or -1 that is not a stylistic choice: nothing stopped the loop. Which bound was it looking at, and could that bound have become huge instead of negative on the way?

Code that is perfect at 5x3 can still hang at 128x1. What is the largest value the variables you count with can hold, and what happens to a test like "i is still below x" the moment such a counter wraps around? Note how close the subject's own defense case, rush(123, 42), already is to one of those ceilings.
rush is called many times in one program, and the defense will call it more than once. Anything you keep between calls -- a static, a global -- has to be left exactly as you found it.
